correctness.rationale: Stationary existence follows from stable critically damped linear convolution with two stationary reset-Brownian drivers having all moments. The exact monomial generator yields nonsingular degree-2/4 systems for every positive reset rate (determinants explicitly factored). The solved variance and fourth moment imply the two-wall kurtosis polynomial. Differentiation yields a degree-9 polynomial with precisely two positive zeros by Descartes (at most two) and sign tests at 1/4,2,10 (at least two); positive denominator fixes complete monotonic intervals. The script reconstructs and verifies the algebra, and an independent regenerative conditional-covariance simulation reproduces representative kurtoses. Nearby-damping persistence uses continuous stationary moments and strict derivative signs, not a conjectured global root count.

originality.rationale: The motivating arXiv article derives the resetting-wall model and two-point chain covariance and reports numerical finite-N kurtosis, but does not supply an exact critically damped one-oscillator fourth-moment polynomial or the double-extremum reset-rate law. General positivity of fourth cumulants for linear Brownian-reset reservoirs, and earlier covariance inversion for a many-oscillator chain, do not imply either quartic rate dependence or the two critical rates. Analogous active-reservoir papers use different non-Gaussian forcing. Priority beyond inspected material remains an independent-review risk.

value.rationale: The motivating paper measures velocity kurtosis numerically to diagnose deviations from thermal Gaussian equilibrium. An exact analysis of the smallest physically natural two-wall critically damped oscillator reveals two rigorously classified rate extrema even while its kinetic energy falls strictly with rate. Thus this is a nontrivial control/diagnostic phase effect not a sign check or routine recomputation of a known table; the stability under nearby damping rules out a purely isolated tuned artifact. It supplies exact benchmark roots and a minimal explanation for reentrant fourth-order fluctuations without claiming general finite-chain behavior.
